habitat: Quiet inland waters, estuaries and coastal pools, always near water. Solitary. It stands in the shallows, walks slowly, or darts and dances after prey.
summary: A white egret, larger and more slender than a Cattle Egret, with a longer black bill and black legs, and yellow feet. Adults normally have head plumes. Breast plumes and back plumes are present only briefly when breeding. The immature lacks plumes.

similar.note: Cattle Egret is smaller, with a short yellow bill and yellow legs, and it follows grazers. Little Egret has a long black bill and yellow feet, and it hunts in the shallows.
Great Egret is much larger, with an orange-yellow bill and black legs and feet. Little Egret has yellow feet only.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^6=64 mature individuals (visiting breeder); paper interval half–double → 32–128.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

head.pattern: Yellow feet. Head plumes are normal. Breast and back plumes are brief and only when breeding.

viewNotes.note: Black bill, black legs and yellow feet, in the shallows.
White head and a long black bill. Adults show head plumes.
White back. Breeding back plumes are brief.
White above. Yellow feet trail behind.

calls.description: Newman does not describe the voice. The texts do not separate the sexes. The catalogue cut is not labelled by sex. Grade A from Vaalkop, South Africa.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman calls it a fairly common resident. Breeding plumes last only briefly, so they were not stored as a summer plumage. Chick down is not described. The call is grade A from Vaalkop.
